# Playbook: ref_commons

When the stock is high (near the cap), take a moderate premium over the stated sustainable share — around 15–25% above. A rich stock can absorb it and the regrowth will bring it back, so you're banking yield while the asset is abundant.

When the stock is stable (hovering at the same level across seasons) and other boats are taking the sustainable share, take a small premium above sustainable each season — around 10–15% above. The stock will dip slightly each round but the 50% regrowth will pull it back, and you're extracting rent from a stable system. Do not sit exactly at the sustainable share in the middle of the game when you can safely take more.

In the final season, go well above sustainable. The only real constraint is that the sum of all boats' catches doesn't exceed the current stock. Estimate what the others will likely take (expect 1.5–2× sustainable from each) and take a large share of what remains. If the stock is high enough that even 2× sustainable per boat won't zero it out, take 2× or more yourself. Do not be conservative in the final season — there is no future to preserve and the yield you leave on the table is gone forever.

When other boats are visibly overfishing (their catches are well above sustainable), resist the urge to match them. The stock is already being drained by their excess; adding your own premium on top accelerates collapse and hurts your future seasons. In this case, stay at or slightly below sustainable to let the stock recover. Once they return to sustainable, resume your small-premium strategy.

When other boats are at or below sustainable and the stock is stable, do not punish yourself by matching their conservatism. The game rewards the one who takes a little more from a stable system.

Track the stock trajectory. A gradual decline (roughly 5–10% over several seasons) is the normal consequence of your premium and does not require pulling back — the stock is still healthy and regrowth is keeping pace. A steep decline (a 20%+ drop in a single season, or a consistent sharp fall over two seasons) signals the stock is being drained faster than it can recover; in that case, pull back to sustainable or below until it stabilizes. If the stock is rising, you have room to take more.

# Playbook: ref_commons

**When it is the first season and the stock is at or near its maximum:**
Take roughly 1.5–2× the sustainable share. The stock is at its ceiling, so you have a buffer. Calculate: if you take X and others take roughly the sustainable share each, the post-regrowth stock is 1.5 × (stock − X − (n−1)×share). Take X large enough to stay above ~80% of maximum stock after regrowth, but don't be timid. A small early lead compounds into a higher total.

**When it is a middle season and the stock is stable or slowly drifting:**
Match the sustainable share or go slightly above it (1.0–1.1×). Do not drop below sustainable in response to a mild decline (a few points over a season) that is driven by others taking slightly above their share. Your own pullback won't offset their surplus, and you forfeit yield for no gain. The stock will hold in a viable plateau as long as total take stays near or just above the regrowth equilibrium. Only drop below sustainable if the decline is steep (>10% in one season) or if you are the one who overfished the prior round.

**When the stock is clearly declining and the cause is broad overfishing:**
Drop to or slightly below the sustainable share for one season to let it recover. This is a short-term sacrifice that preserves future yield. Do not extend this beyond one or two seasons unless the stock is truly crashing.

**When it is the final season:**
Go hard. There is no regrowth and no future cost. Estimate what the other boats will take based on their recent history (use their last 2–3 seasons' average). Take: stock − (their estimated total) − a small safety buffer of 5–10. This is almost always far more than 2.5× sustainable. For example, if stock is 80 and others average ~10 each, take 50–55, not 25–30. The single biggest mistake in this game is under-fishing the final season out of residual caution. The only real constraint is that total take must not exceed the stock (or you get nothing). If you are uncertain whether others will also go greedy, take stock/2 as a floor — that is still usually double or triple the sustainable share.

**General monitoring rule:**
Each season, compare the stock to the previous season. Stable → maintain or push slightly. Rising → push above sustainable. Falling → check whether you caused it or others did; only pull back if you are the driver. The stock level is your primary signal; the "sustainable share" is a reference point, not a ceiling.

**What not to do:**
- Do not drop below sustainable in a middle season just because the stock dipped a few points while others were the ones overshooting. You will not fix their problem by starving yourself, and you will lose points.
- Do not play the final season with the same logic as the middle. The preservation argument evaporates on the last round. If you catch yourself thinking "I should leave some for regrowth" in the final season, you are making an error.

# Playbook: Ref Commons

**When I'm shown the stock and the sustainable share, I calculate the safe upper bound for my catch as: stock minus (number of other boats × a reasonable per-boat catch).** This tells me how much I can actually take without risking a crash.

**In non-final seasons, I default to the sustainable share.** This keeps the stock stable and preserves my future harvests. The small short-term gain from overfishing is rarely worth the compounding loss of a shrinking stock. Confirmed: holding at sustainable for 5 straight seasons kept the stock in a narrow, stable band.

**When another boat is clearly overfishing (catching well above sustainable) while I'm at sustainable, I stay at sustainable rather than matching them.** Overfishing in response to overfishing accelerates stock decline. If the overfisher moderates (as they often do once the stock visibly drops), I've preserved the stock. If they don't, I've at least not made it worse. Confirmed: a boat took 20 vs sustainable 11 in season 1, then moderated to ~9-10 for the rest of the game.

**I track whether other boats are converging toward cooperation.** If two or more boats have been at or near the sustainable share for 2+ consecutive seasons, I treat the group as cooperative and can plan my final-season move on that assumption.

**In the final season, I catch significantly more than the sustainable share.** I calculate my target as: stock minus (2 × the highest reasonable catch I expect from the other boats). If they've been cooperative for multiple seasons, I estimate their final-season catch at 1–1.5× sustainable. My safe ceiling is then stock minus 2× that estimate. I take most of the surplus up to that ceiling. A fixed multiplier of 2–3× sustainable is too conservative when the stock is healthy and others have a long cooperative record — it leaves substantial value unclaimed.

**In the final season, I do not try to take everything.** My ceiling assumes at least one other boat may defect moderately (up to ~2× sustainable). I size my catch so that even if one other boat doubles, total catch stays below the stock. This is the risk I accept; I don't plan for both others to defect maximally.

**I never let the stock drop below 60% of its starting value.** At that point, the sustainable share is shrinking fast and the risk of a cascade to zero rises sharply. If the stock is declining because others are overfishing and I have seasons left, I consider whether I can profitably stay out (catch 0) to let regrowth recover the stock, rather than harvesting a shrinking pool.

**I read the stock trajectory, not just the current number.** If the stock has been flat or growing for several seasons, the system is stable and I can be confident in my sustainable-share strategy. If it's declining, I need to recalculate and either reduce my catch or prepare for a shorter effective game.
